source_read: PDF of the accepted manuscript (Drug Test Anal, doi:10.1002/dta.2300), AM pp. 1-35 all read (text, references, figure captions, Tables 1-2); Figures 1-2 (AM pp. 28-29) checked on rendered pages; no journal pagination, so pages are given as AM p. N (PDF page).

claims.note: Philp supports these parts of the joint second-hand sentence: colour tests are presumptive; other substances react with the Marquis reagent, including aspirin and sugar (one cited reference); more than one drug or tablet colouring agents can affect the result; visual spot tests are qualitative. It does not support 'MDMA, MDEA and MDA give similar colours': it gives only MDA (black) for the Marquis reagent and no MDMA or MDEA colour (text, Table 1, Figures 1-2), so that part rests on Winstock alone. On 'no amount': Philp also reports that camera-based (RGB) analysis of Marquis and Simon's results was semi-quantitative and agreed with GC data, and that a sol-gel Simon's sensor with digital colorimetry gave quantitative results (laboratory methods, not kits read by eye), so 'by eye' would make the sentence exact. Philp's harm-reduction paragraph relays Murray et al. (2003), the claim's own primary study, so it is not independent support. Philp is a forensic, law-enforcement-oriented narrative review with no stated search method.

anchors.extracted: Colour tests are now used strictly for presumptive identification of controlled substances; they were the most common screening method in a UNODC exercise of 181 laboratories.

Qualitative presumptive tests indicate the presence or absence of a drug class; confirmatory laboratory analysis identifies all components and quantifies drugs; colorimetric (camera) analysis has shown potential for semi-quantitative results.

anchors.locator: Chemistry of common color tests > General screening reagents, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The Marquis reagent, first developed for morphine and other alkaloids, reacts with many drug classes (orange-brown with amphetamine, black with MDA, olive-green with 3,4-dimethoxymethamphetamine); other compounds also react, including aspirin and sugar; opium alkaloids give a purple product.

Presumptive results can be affected by the presence of more than one drug or by colouring agents used in tablets such as ecstasy and piperazines; Scott's test gave false positives with cutting agents.

anchors.locator: Advances in color testing > Digital image analysis, 1st-2nd paragraphs; Solid sensors, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Colour readings are subjective, depending on the reader's vision and the lighting; digital RGB analysis of Marquis and Simon's results was semi-quantitative and agreed with gas chromatography; a sol-gel Simon's sensor with digital colorimetry gave quantitative results.

Relays Murray's evaluation of MDMA screening kits (should not be used by the public; pure and adulterated forms not distinguished) and a review that rated colour tests the best low-technology option for point-of-care drug checking while recommending handheld infrared or Raman instruments.
The authors call the belief that colour tests give simple binary, easy-to-read outcomes a common misconception and stress awareness of false positives.

key_findings.correction: Matches AM p. 4; no MDMA or methamphetamine colour is given anywhere in text, tables or figures.
Simon's 'distinguishes primary and secondary amines' is in the Table 1 continuation on AM p. 34.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed on the rendered Figure 3b (AM p. 30): the nitro groups are drawn 1,3 (m-dinitrobenzene).

missed: AM p. 2 (Introduction, 3rd paragraph), AM p. 13 (Digital image analysis, 2nd paragraph) and AM p. 15 (Solid sensors, 1st paragraph): camera-based RGB analysis of Marquis and Simon's results was semi-quantitative and agreed with gas chromatography, and a sol-gel Simon's sensor with digital colorimetry gave quantitative results. Relevant to any claim that colour tests show no amount: true for reading by eye, not for these laboratory methods.
